Mr. Chairman, before clause 2 is passed, and since the Prime Minister is in the house, I am wondering if it would not be advisable to stand clause 2 until the next federal-provincial conference is over.
We know that two days ago the Quebec premier accused the federal government of aggression because it had invaded the field of education which comes under provincial jurisdiction and because it was trying, without prior consultation with the provinces, to include words such as national unity.
If clause 2 were passed on the eve of the opening of that federal-provincial conference, that would be, Mr. Chairman, sheer provocation as far as the Quebec government is concerned. In the circumstances, and if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) are really sincere, it seems to me that the clear and definite objection expressed by the Quebec government as to preliminary consultations before a hasty passing of the bill should be taken into consideration, and I wonder whether it would not be better to defer consideration of clause 2.
We can pass on to other clauses. There is clause 3 and about 50 other clauses to pass in Bill No. C-163 and they will certainly not be agreed to before the end of the federal-provincial conference. If, during the conference, there are consultations about this bill, it will then be possible to submit amendments. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the government would be wise to stand clause 2, in order to comply with the representations of the provincial governments demanding that consultations be held before a too hasty passage of this bill.

I would not make such a proposal if there were still a month to elapse before the federal-provincial conference, but since it is our last sitting before the opening of that federal provincial conference, I feel that it is essential.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to dwell on the matter, but I think it would be advisable to stand this clause. I think that the government should accept this suggestion. It would be an indication of its good faith and good intentions, while the contrary could be considered as an act of provocation or paternalistism. It would mean that the clause would be passed without any consideration being given to the representations of the provincial governments, even if a meeting has been arranged in the hope of reaching an agreement. In fact, this would be the same as saying: "A decision has been made and we go ahead". This is more or less what the hasty passing of clause 2 would imply.

By the then minister of transport. He is more important than the department.

I can only say there is a new Minister of Transport now. But the hon. gentleman is well aware that there will be a new board, whatever may be its name, with its own responsibility to follow the legislation which this house enacts. It will be bound by whatever regulations and structure are given to it by orders in council. I cannot tell the hon. gentleman what may happen in the next few months. The minister has said that the board will be bound by the legislation passed by this house and added that it will also be bound by orders in council passed in the future. I am glad to have that assurance from her, though I know Hansard cannot be considered as a legal document and is not binding in courts of law. The minister of transport of the day assumed a great deal of authority for himself on July 22, 1964, because he said there was no regulation of C.A.T.V. And that great god of the radio world, R. M. Fowler, made some comments in his 1965 report on broadcasting. He said:
Our terms of reference specifically excluded community antenna services.
Then he went on to make many references to them, stating that the radio and television world lacked legal authority to control them and that something had to be done. Now that C.A.T.V. applications are to fall within the jurisdiction of the broadcasting council, as I will call it for the moment, and since clause 2(c) has been amended and we believe there will be reasonable men on the board, we expect the legislation of this parliament to kill deader than a dodo the autocratic statement of the minister of transport on July 22, 1964.

If an act of parliament does not kill that statement there is no use in parliament passing acts at all; ministers can simply issue statements which will have the force of law. I will accept what has been said by the Secretary of State that the new board will be bound by the legislation of parliament and by the orders in council which may be issued, and I am certain that this means free and open hearings of all C.A.T.V. applications as suggested, though rather indirectly, in subclauses 3(c) and 3(d). Clause 3(c) reads:
-"broadcasting licence" or.. ."licence" means a licence to carry on a broadcasting undertaking issued under this Act;
Then clause 3(d) goes on to say that a broadcasting undertaking includes a broadcasting transmitting undertaking. While reception is entirely different from broadcasting, the two are inextricably involved and since in clause 19 it is stated that a public hearing shall be held by the council in connection with the issue of a broadcasting licence I take it, and I wish it to be on record in Hansard if nowhere else, that there will be public hearings in connection with the issue of a broadcasting licence, and under 3(d) a broadcasting undertaking includes a broadcasting receiving undertaking.

Mr. Chairman, just a word to explain why the text of the amendment is unacceptable.
It is exactly as if it was stated in a statute that in order to be appointed to a position a person must be competent. More and more and according to the spirit of the Bill of Rights the use of both languages is accepted in federal institutions. Therefore, if it is stated in a statute that a certain senior official must have sufficient knowledge of the other language, that is equal to saying that to accede to this or that post one must be competent. That is a useless repetition. The spirit of the amendment is acceptable but what becomes somewhat unthinkable is to include in a statute, as the hon. member seems to indicate, such or such a degree of competence.
It is obvious that to obtain a senior appointment, one must be competent. It is more and more evident that a position like that one calls for an adequate knowledge of both languages. It is not necessary to stipulate it in the act; it would be redundancy.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks on that subject. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) says that it is more and more an acknowledged fact that to be able to express oneself in both languages in a federal government agency is a proof of competence. If such were the case in practice, if the usual practice and tradition had been such in the past, I do not say that the hon. member for Lotbiniere would not be right, but precisely tradition did not accustom us to that.
I read recently in Hansard an answer to a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). A list of the directors of each crown corporation and government board was given mentioning the number of those who were bilingual, English-speaking or French-speaking. I was surprised to see that still today, a year after our centennial, there were several boards and crown corporations without any French speaking director.
It is precisely due to such facts, that I have deemed it advisable to present that amendment. Perhaps in a general policy statement, the hon. member for Lotbiniere would rightly mention that it is a matter of competence, but the fact is not always recognized. We now have evidence thereof based on figures and facts. I do not remember on what date, this answer appeared in Hansard. That is why I cannot give the figures but during the lunch hour, I will probably check on it and bring down something more definite.
But the facts have proven and still prove, through a reply given less than a month ago to a question on the order paper that within crown corporations and government bodies, this knowledge of qualification evaluation was not always observed.
In the circumstances and since the facts are so contrary to the principle mentioned by the member for Lotbiniere, I believe that he should make an effort-it should not be too difficult for him-to force the government to practise what it so highly preaches.
It is one of the objectives of my amendment and I am surprised that the member for Lotbiniere should object. He claims that writing it out in the bill does not mean anything. I believe it does, precisely because the facts have shown that we are justified in asking that it be written into the bill. If it is written into the bill, then we can say it is compulsory. The Canadian Bill of Rights is not in the act, in the constitution and the Minister of Justice says that if it were included in the

constition, it would have force of law and be much more valuable. That is the argument brought forth by the Minister of Justice.
Well, I think the same thing applies to bilingualism; if it were written into the legislation, it would have force of law and it would be much more valuable and could not be evaded.
I wonder why the hon. member for Lotbiniere objects to having it written into the act, for the same reason as the Minister of Justice wants the Bill of Rights to be written down in the legislation, in the constitution.
This argument of the Minister of Justice brings down the whole argument of the member for Lotbiniere and it is the best reference I can give him. That is why I submit the amendment is necessary to correct the present situation and all should make it a duty to support it.

Mr. Chairman, this clause makes it clear that the proposed commission is obligated to implement the broadcasting policy set out in clause 2 of the bill. I would like to direct the attention of the committee specifically to subclause (e) of clause 2, which has already been accepted by the committee. It is stated there:

Later in clause 2(g) we find the following:
(g) the national broadcasting service should-
(ii) be extended to all parts of Canada, as public funds become available.
This is not a new obligation. It is a restatement of something that has been implicit in all legislation since governments assumed full responsibility for public broadcasting more than 35 years ago. I only hope that in a much shorter period of time this obligation will be discharged. I trust that the legislation now before us will help to fill a gap that the
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has allowed to exist over the years.
The particular situation to which I draw attention is the broadcasting void existing in northern Saskatchewan, northeastern Alberta and the adjacent Northwest Territories. This whole vast region, a storehouse of national resources and the home of thousands of good Canadian citizens, has been shunted aside time and again by the C.B.C. in its development of broadcasting facilities. It is the area referred to in the Fowler report of 1965 as "the forgotten north." I draw the attention of the committee to the wording of this bill. In clause 15 and in clause 2 the service owed this area is clearly stated as a right.
In my own constituency a large proportion of the people have no television service whatever. One example is the lie a la Crosse area. Also, over a large area even the radio broadcast service ranges from indifferent to poor. Over the years the people there have been told that they must be patient, that service would be provided but that high costs and other priorities were holding up extension of service to the north. Perhaps there was a day when this sort of excuse was valid, but it cannot be accepted today.
While more than 10,000 people in my small area are without even black and white television service and suffer from inadequate radio service, the rest of Canada has the luxury of colour television. In my area the fishermen, farmers, forest workers, miners and all the companies large and small for which many of them work, pay taxes that go to pay the cost of providing broadcasting services. These services are supposed to be national in scope. They are not supposed to be selective, restricted only to those areas of dense population and easy terrain.
When 60 per cent of Canadians have access to two or more television channels surely it is not too much to ask that the people of my area, and the people of the north generally, be provided with at least one. The Fowler commission of 1965 recognized the justice of this plea. It agreed that it was a matter of urgency and fairness. In its recommendations it gave top priority to the extension of adequate facilities to the north. Only recently the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development emphasized that it is necessary to supply proper broadcasting service to the north if people and industry are to be attracted to the north and expected to stay there.
I had occasion to deal with this matter once before in this chamber, as reported on page

6306	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting 2654 of Hansard for March 14, 1966. At that time I hoped that the C.B.C., if it would not heed my words, would at least heed those of the Fowler commission and of a minister of the crown. But nothing happened. The forgotten north remains forgotten at C.B.C. headquarters. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and myself now have one thing in common. We are equally ignored. I hope that with the new wind blowing through the corridors of C.B.C. headquarters, with a new president and with a new policy directive from parliament the C.B.C. will now undertake the work that should have been done years ago.
At page 194 of the Fowler commission report there is a recommendation that additional operating costs for the northern services be raised by $500,000 a year and that the northern service budget be increased by $1.7 million. This sounds like a great deal of money, and it is. But when one considers the amount of tax money yielded by the area about which I am talking and the ease with which almost twice that amount has been found for enterprises such as the Company of Young Canadians, one feels that such an outlay would be a modest one to ensure fair treatment for a large group of Canadians and the faithful carrying out of broadcasting policy as approved by parliament. It seems to me it would be only simple justice to find a mere one and a half million dollars for a basic northern service when tens of millions of dollars are so readily found to extend colour television service to other segments of the population which already have one, two or more black and white channels from which to choose.

Mr. Chairman, when this bill was sent to the standing committee it contained a provision empowering the regulatory authority to make regulations respecting scheduling in relation to any category or

categories of programs. The committee discussed this at length. It was suggested that this regulatory power probably was impractical and in any case was unnecessary since it was thought that the desired effect could be achieved through the power to determine the conditions of licence. For that reason the committee proposed and passed an amendment to the effect that this provision should be deleted from the bill.
While this was the thought of the committee, what was overlooked in the discussion was that this would cause a rigidity in the system which is undesirable because it would mean that conditions could not be altered except at five year intervals. Further, although clause 63 provides for the continuation of regulations made by the B.B.G. under the 1958 act, there is some question whether such regulations would be valid if they dealt with subjects not specifically covered by regulatory powers in the new legislation.
The key to this situation lies in subclause 2(d) which already has been agreed to by this committee. It is clear that the new regulatory authority must have power to implement the national broadcasting policy in all its aspects. I should like to remind members that subclause 2(d), which is an essential element of the national broadcasting policy, declares that the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should be varied and comprehensive and should provide reasonable, balanced opportunity for the expression of differing views on matters of public concern. It goes on further to provide that the programming shall be of high standard, using predominantly Canadian creative and other resources.
It seems that the committee inadvertently did drop something essential. I am therefore prepared to have an amendment moved which would add to subclause 16(l)(b)(i) the following:
-and the allocation of broadcasting time for the purpose of giving effect to paragraph (d) of section 2.
This would then mean that the subclause would read as follows:
-the council may make regulations "respecting standards of programs and the allocation of broadcasting time for the purpose of giving effect to paragraph (d) of section 2."

The same is true of telephone service, for instance. We say that there will be only one telephone company in a town, to avoid the necessity of installing two series of posts and wires, to avoid the necessity of installing two series of posts and wires, to avoid unnecessary expenses. grounds that there are no more wavelengths available. Competition does not exist any more. Mr. Chairman, may I continue my explanations?
It is known for a fact that today there is practically no competition, especially in the field of television. There is only one private station, that is all, in any one area or municipality. That station can ask any rate it wishes from the advertiser or sponsor of television programs. There is hardly no competition and that of the C.B.C. is gradually decreasing in the commercial field. Because the station is the only one, or almost, it lacks competition-except in large centres such as Toronto and Montreal, the licensee can ask the sponsor whatever rates and tariffs it chooses.
In the last few years, the rates and tariffs of television or radio licensees have increased rather rapidly. All this, naturally, is part of the advertising budget of a company, and that is one of the main reasons for the recent increases in rates. If a broadcaster had to justify an increase in the rates or tariffs he charges his sponsors, these increases would often be rejected, or if they were accepted it would be because the private broadcaster had improved the quality of his programs. It is obvious that the profits made by television stations today are very high in comparison
6310	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting with investments, and the reason for this is that there is little or no competition, it having been eliminated either by the law itself or by the small number of frequencies.
Any person cannot get a licence to operate a radio or television station No. It is limited, very limited indeed. Anyone can launch out into running a newspaper; one does not need a licence for that, and whoever wants to can become owner of a newspaper or start a newspaper. There is no limitation in the field of newspapers, but there is in the field of television and radio. First, a wave-length must be available, and then a licence has to be obtained from the Canadian broadcasting council. If competition is eliminated, unfair advantage is taken of the people by a company which, according to the law, no longer has any competition. It is at that time that the public must be protected, and to do that, since favours are bestowed on the licensee, he has to justify his request to increase his rates. [DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I believe it is absolutely normal, but, the radio and television stations may not like it. It is as if we were to say to bus companies which have the exclusive transportation rights between two towns: You may ask the prices you see fit. Needless to say, these companies having no competitors would increase their prices immediately.
In the radio and television field, the same problem exists. If the government eliminates all competition by limiting the number of licences, it must also eliminate the exploitation of the public by requiring the station owners to submit any increase in rates to the approval of the Canadian radio commission.
That is the purpose of my amendment and I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that it will inevitably result-and that is a very important point to consider-in a general improvement of the quality of the programs produced by the private stations because, given their very high margin of profit, they will never be able to get increases in their rates or tariffs now, unless the quality of their programming increases considerably.
Mr. Chairman, I feel this is a very normal request, and there is no precedent involved: Such is already the case for electric power companies, telephone companies, trucking companies, passenger service companies, in all fields, in fact, where the government has established a ceiling on the number of licences. The only field where this was not the case was broadcasting, and it is time for this restriction is to be imposed. That is my reason for moving this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, the question introduced by the hon. member for Lapointe raises the subject of whether the regulatory authority is to be a price setting agency. It seems to me that is a very important principle which is worthy of debate, but not at this point when we are dealing with this subclause. There is one aspect of it, however, that does concern me. We have been concerned about the monopoly control of media in this country. There is no problem in this connection in the large centres where there are newspapers and more than one television or radio station.
It seems to me there could be a danger in some of the smaller centres in which there is only one television station. Access to this station could be denied to a political candidate or a person in business either by refusing to sell time or quoting that person discriminatory rates. I think we should be concerned about this. Is there anything in the legislation whereby a person who is treated that way could have recourse to the authority if he met with an outright denial of time or if he could prove the station owner had set a price on the time which was not the same as that charged to others and was such as to discourage him? We do have to face the fact that some people have a monopoly on television broadcasting in certain areas. It seems to me that everyone who applies for the use of time should be treated equally. Is there anything in the bill which would provide some course of action to a person who felt he was not justly dealt with by a station owner?

I cannot think of any place, Mr. Chairman, that there would be any such provision unless it would be in the renewal of licence provision. I think quicker action

would probably be gained by recourse to the public press or other media to indicate this situation. No doubt such action would result in the council or commission getting in touch with the offending station. I do not believe there would be anything in the act which would permit definite sanctions except at the time of the renewal of the licence. I do not believe anyone should for a moment discount that provision because it is a rather important factor. In the first place, the public outcry which my hon. friend or anyone like him who was discriminated against would make, would be very considerable. This kind of discriminatory action would, I think, be something which would cause an individual not to have his licence renewed. He would have to have very strong justification for the action and I doubt that he could find justification for it.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about that amendment which seems very logical to me.
Mr. Chairman, there are obvious, I would even say gross, abuses in that field at the present time. Some television and radio stations which have no competition are asking very high prices from some and lower prices from others.
To put something on tape, for instance, some television stations might charge up to $300 while others will charge $35 for the same work. It is the same thing for television and radio programs. It is a matter of viewing hours and there are certainly gross abuses there. Since there is no competition or hardly any, as stated by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), I think that it would be very important to find a way to prevent the private stations which have no competitors from exploiting the public.
The public is often exploited; quite often, when we want to use this mass media, we are told: Well, my dear Sir, for you it is such and such a price; you can take it or leave it. For another person, it may be cheaper, but for you, you must take it or leave it.
There are certainly manifest abuses and I think the hon. member for Lapointe is right in moving such an amendment. I think this amendment should be considered thoroughly. It would be logical also that the government should control the air waves and the use of certain wave-lengths, because of the scarcity of frequencies. I think the prices also should be controlled as well as increases. When the owners of such mass media increase their prices, the commission should be informed
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting and the price increases should not be allowed if they are not warranted or if they are prohibitive.
The commission should have some control. There are certainly some abuses. Private initiative is good. We agree 100 per cent with private enterprise, but we do not want it to go too far; when it is harmful to the community, or to certain institutions, it is time for the state to step in. Then it is the responsibility of the state to intervene, under these conditions, and I am sure something can be done, because abuses are apparent. Somebody ought to deal with such abuses. The rent control board has been set up and yet, the situation in this field is much less serious than in the broadcasting field.
There are all types of controls, but there is no control possible without competition. As far as rents are concerned, there is much competition. If accommodations prove unsatisfactory, there are others to be found.
But in the present instance, if we are dissatisfied, we must yield or do without, because there is nothing else. I feel therefore that, as far as public services are concerned, the people should be in a position to make reasonable and proper use thereof.
Some individuals wield such power that they can tell someone they do not like too much: the price is so much, take it or leave it. There is no discussion possible, there is nothing to be done. Then, I believe the commission should intervene in those cases and I agree 100 per cent with the hon. member for Lapointe. I also ask the members of this house-it seems very important to me-to make an effort to find a solution to this problem.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, very briefly I wonder whether the hon. member for Lapointe would consider amending his motion to provide that the commission be empowered to set a maximum instead of setting a whole tariff? If that were done I think it would find acceptance here. It does seem to me to be rather dangerous to ask the commission to establish all rates at all levels for radio and television stations.

Mr. Chairman, I think it would be most difficult to ask the council to set a maximum rate, because conditions vary from one area to the next, from one station to another.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Some stations will produce very good programs which, obviously, will cost more than showing films. That is why no general rule can be set.
In some areas, it would be more expensive, because ratings are higher, the T.V. antenna is more powerful and more expensive and the operating costs are heavier. maximum rates, even if later on the companies are required to justify the increases they request.
I am willing to change the amendment in the way suggested by the hon. member for Kamloops.

If the

Mr. Chairman, while the hon. member for Lapointe is looking over the amendment I should like to ask a question on paragraph (vii), which reads:
-with the approval of the Treasury Board, fixing the schedules of fees to be paid by licensees and providing for the payment thereof,
I have often wondered just what revenue is received from the licensing of radio and television stations. Is the minister in a position to give the committee any information in this regard? How is that revenue determined? Can she give some examples of the amounts that various licensees have to pay for the use of the airwaves for periods of time?
Mr. Chairman, I do not happen to know but I could find out for the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to know whether this clause includes the licensing of community antenna television and the establishment of fees for such service. If so, what arrangements are made to cover closed circuit television broadcasts?

Mr. Chairman, closed circuit television does not pick programs out of the air and therefore is not covered by the broadcasting legislation. If it did do so then it would be covered. These licensing arrangements apply to all broadcasting undertakings that are covered, including C.A.T.V.

Is it not the intention of the minister to cover closed circuit community antenna services as well as those that pick programs out of the air? Also, may I ask how extensive are the regulations that are proposed in connection with this fight that has been going on for a long time about United States programs that can be picked up close to the border but which can only be received in Timiskaming, for example,

through a community antenna system? Apparently these antennas can reproduce a fairly weak signal which is then fed into a closed circuit.
Mr. Chairman, there does not appear to be any constitutional basis upon which the federal government can legislate with respect to closed circuit television.

There may not be many closed circuit television receivers in my area, but for the last 12 years there has been one that does rebroadcast programs. Let me give an example. It can take another station's program and rebroadcast it on a closed circuit, using its own camera to dub in an advertisement in the middle of the program. Therefore I presume that some regulations will be in effect and I am wondering how extensive they will be. To date there has not appeared to be any such regulation. The Department of Transport will look into cases of interference or where there is an outright theft of another station's program for advertising purposes, but it seems to me there must be some regulation in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, two of the questions that have been considered are, first of all, program integrity; you are not to use somebody else's advertising on your own programs. Second, at present one must carry the national program that is available in the area. Aside from those two considerations, I can say nothing more. I have been visited by C.A.T.V. operators and both of these matters were discussed. They were well aware that these would be two of the requirements. In addition, because their operation is quite different from that of an ordinary broadcasting station the regulations will be tailor made to suit their operations instead of having general regulations made applicable to all.

Is it the intention of the government to limit the number of programs that can be picked up and rebroadcast in a given area? That has been one difficulty. In addition, many of these stations are not licensed by the Department of Transport. Are they now going to be able to carry whatever programs they can pick up by means of a community antenna system and rebroadcast them, in some cases on closed circuit television, without a licence?

I am afraid I am somewhat confused by my hon. friend. I said we do not grant licences for closed circuits except with

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting respect to C.A.T.V. operations which take programs from the air. I am not sure if I understand what the hon. member is saying. If the hon. member is saying that these people are actually broadcasting from their studio, then of course, they will have to get a licence for that kind of broadcasting undertaking.

But they are not broadcasting over the air. This is not a television station but a service provided by means of coaxial cable. That cable is already carrying one or two channels to the community antenna. The studio will transmit over the coaxial cable and they will not, in that sense, be transmitting over the air. Mr. Chairman, just a few words in reply to the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters).
I will tell him that all the closed circuit stations now in operation have to hold a licence. Mr. Chairman, clause 16 is not one of the clauses that I asked yesterday to

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting be stood. I am indebted to the committee for having stood clauses 3, 19, 28 and 47, as I desired yesterday afternoon. Since clause 16 was stood I should like to make a few comments in support of the hon. member for Lapointe, inasmuch as he is endeavouring to control the advertising rates charged on television or radio stations.
From listening to him carefully it is quite clear that his agile and alert mind has picked up a point which has not been considered by those who framed this radio and broadcasting bill in quiet and had it printed and put before members of parliament to push through. But I believe the hon. member for Lapointe is weeping on cold shoulders, or should I say, casting his message on stony ground.
I am sure that when the hon. member for Lapointe was attending the Jesuit college in Quebec he must have heard our Lord's parable about the sower. A sower cast some seed on fertile ground and it sprang up and multiplied a hundredfold. But some seed fell among thorns and the thorns sprang up and choked the seed. Other seed fell on stony ground and was burned by the sun. If the hon. member for Lapointe intimates that the holder of a television licence is in a monopoly position in setting advertising rates, he is 100 per cent correct. But that is the situation you put yourself in when you grant monopoly television licences.
Many markets can only support one television licence. The hon. member for Kamloops stood in his place just now and said that the competition of the market place will control the rates as one television station competes with another. That applies to Toronto, Montreal and some other centres where there is more than one television station. But in the advertising world, if a monopoly situation develops in some centre the situation is different. Take Pembroke, Ontario, which is handy and has only got one television station. If the hon. member for Lapointe thinks that in a monopoly situation the advertising rates are going to go sky high, unless controlled, I feel he is on fair ground in that assumption.
The hon. member for Lapointe seems to have overlooked the important fact that an advertiser does not have to use the local television station in Pembroke. There is a newspaper there and you can use sign boards, or individually painted signs and put them in store windows, or you can have them with posts in the centre. Or you can get advertisements printed by some publisher and mail them through the post office. There are other


competitive ways of getting advertising done. If you do not use the television station the owner will lower his rates so that you will leave these other forms of competitive media and give him the advertising revenue that he sees going to other avenues.
But if my hon. friend for Lapointe is intimating that the cabinet might take some action to control the advertising rates on television stations when they are in a monopoly position, he is really sowing his seed on stony ground, especially when you consider what has happened to the general public at airports in the carriage of passengers to the city that the airport is serving. On Monday of this week I was on a train for some hours with a member of the present cabinet. During the long train ride-I was on the train because no airplanes were flying that day-the cabinet minister remarked to me that he had recently flown from Montreal to Toronto and he had not been met as prearranged and so had taken the monopoly cab service, so magnificently provided by the Department of Transport, to downtown Toronto. He informed me that he pretty nearly had to wire his bank to see if he had enough money to cover the cheque he had to issue to pay for the ride. I said to this cabinet minister: "What are you kicking about? The Minister of Transport okayed these rates and nobody can cast any aspersions on the fairness of any rates when this cabinet okays them, I'm sure." All he did was smile.
When the hon. member for Lapointe says there should be some control over the rates charged for advertising by television stations in a monopoly situation, I have to agree with him. But I must point out that in the advertising world there are competitive avenues of advertising open to the businessman. He does not have to use the local television station.
Will the hon. member allow me a question?
I certainly will, to you.
You are going steady, you two, aren't you?

You will admit also that the minister who used a means of transportation which has the monopoly between the Toronto airport and his home had other ways of getting home. He did not have to take the official limousine. He could have walked, that is another way. Therefore, it is the same thing in the field of advertising.

Mr. Chairman, as I said before, the hon. member for Lapointe has an alert and agile mind and he gave us an example of this just now. I intended to refer to the fact that there was a competitive source of transportation available to the cabinet minister. He could have stood at Malton for about three-quarters of an hour after telephoning for a taxi to come and get him or he could have walked the 14 miles to downtown and save the money.
But I wanted to make some reference to the statement by the hon. member for Kamloops, who referred to the free play of the market place. That phrase was used a good deal on this side of the house when we were setting up the consumer affairs department. The free play of the marketplace would keep prices down; the cost of living would fall and everybody would be happy, happy, happy from now on because we have a new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
It seems too bad that the hon. member for Lapointe should be the one to put his finger on such a glaring oddity as this, that a monopoly television operator in one of the smaller centres of Canada can charge as much as he likes. Now the suggestion is made that we cannot set rates but can only specify a maximum figure. I have been in business long enough to know that the maximum rate is always the only one at which an operator can make a profit; anything lower and he would be running in the red.
Something should be done to deal with this question and I admire the hon. member for Lapointe for putting his finger on the spot where action is called for. If the cabinet is disposed to accept the suggestion by the hon. member for Lapointe that there should be control over the rates charged by television stations, I hope my hon. friends will accept the argument that there should be control exercised over the exorbitant rates charged by monopoly cab operators at airports. At the present time the Minister of Transport is the only authority that can exercise control over these rates which are so high that, as one cabinet minister said to me recently, one almost has to wire the bank to see whether one has enough money to pay the fare demanded. I do not know how many hon. members are aware that it costs as much to take a monopoly cab from Malton airport to the eastern boundary of Scarborough as it does to fly from Toronto to Ottawa.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, we have listened to this not very honourable member ad nauseam and I would ask that he be requested to stick to the point he is supposed to be discussing. Mr. Chairman, I have considered this, the department has considered it and so have other people. It does not simply spring out of nowhere. We would have to impose individual tariffs on each one of them and the schedule would have to change as circumstances change. The

Mr. Chairman, I think that the remarks of the hon. member for York-Humber were pertinent, in that the field of radio and television constitutes a monopoly and a state licence is necessary to broadcast programs.
[Miss LaMarsh.l
DEBATES	February 2, 1968
Now, the Secretary of State says that if we had to create a board to control prices or set rates for radio and television stations, that would involve a great deal of work, since the situation changes in each case and there are many radio and television stations.
On that point, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out two things to the Secretary of State: first, I would like to give as an example the trucking industry. There are many more trucking enterprises than radio or television companies. Yet there is a transport commission which sets prices for trucking enterprises in each case, according to the distance travelled and the area involved.
This could, in the trucking industry, mean twenty times more work than it would in the field of broadcasting. However, it is done in order to prevent a monopoly from exploiting the public, even if there are perhaps ten times as many trucking companies as there are television or radio stations. That is why I say to the hon. Secretary of State that her argument that this would mean to much work does not hold when it is a question of protecting the public against a monopoly allowed by law.
Second, Mr. Chairman, the hon. Secretary of State said that the problem received consideration but that there are no provisions dealing with this in the bill. I think it would not be difficult to include such a provision. Otherwise, broadcasting will be the only field where licences are issued and where there is no price control board. This would be the only field where competition would be limited by virtue of a licence, without there being at the same time a board which establishes rates.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Now, if the minister feels that this should not be the responsibility of the Canadian radio commission, it could be entrusted to the transport commission. Since it is the Department of Transport which, in the end, has to pass on the plans submitted for a radio or television station, let the transport commission deal with the matter of rates tariffs to be set for private radio and television stations, just as it deals, for instance, with the matter of the rates of the Bell Telephone Company or other independent telephone companies.
Such is the principle according to which, when the state restricts competition, it must also restrict the rates of those monopolies to prevent them from taking advantage of the public.
February 2, 1968

Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I think that the argument of the Secretary of State does not hold for the two above-mentioned reasons. In the first place, it would not involve so much work since the transport commission does it for transportation companies which are more numerous than radio and television stations. Then, it is the only field where rates are unlimited while the government is restricting competition.
I hope that the Secretary of State will accept at least the principle involved, even though afterwards she may hand over the control to the council.
That is why, at the request of the hon. members for Kamloops and Halifax (Messrs. Fulton and McCleave), I changed my amendment by adding a third subclause to clause 16 which reads as follows:
(3) (a) The council will be authorized to establish a maximum scale for the rates and tariffs charged by the broadcasters or licencees. The council shall hold public meetings to consider any application for increases in the rates and tariffs charged by the broadcasters or licensees unless authorized by the council following such public hearings.

If this kind of amendment is not accepted I wonder how the minister intends to handle the sort of situation which developed in northern Ontario where a private community antenna operator got a licence in an area very remote from a broadcasting station. People subscribing to his service were charged a $200 connection fee and had to pay $5 per month rental. If a family moved out of a house the incoming family also had to pay the $200 connection fee, and one instance was reported to me of a house which changed occupancy five times in a year and each time the $200 fee was charged. When we give such a person a licence I think we have an obligation to protect his customers. The situation has improved following the installation of a C.B.C. repeater station, and CFCL has installed a satellite in the Hearst area. Originally Port Arthur and Fort William had to supply the coverage through community antenna. The $200 fee was an unreasonable charge. If a maximum is not imposed then an unscrupulous person will have the right to charge whatever the traffic will bear.
My experience with television has not been that bad. A television station operator charges for national advertising on the basis of audience coverage and there is another rate for local advertising. But in northern Canada such an operator could eliminate competition
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting by the rates he charges, raising them or lowering them to suit his own purposes. It does not seem unreasonable to me to stipulate a maximum connection fee and a maximum monthly rate for C.A.T.V., and I would not object if the maximum set in northern areas were twice as high as the average in other areas. Prior to this the government had no control over such rates, and I know that the Department of Transport would have been glad to have some kind of control to prevent such abuses taking place. In fact there was no control until the C.B.C. or some other entrepreneur provided alternate service.

The hon. member should not forget that for the first time in this bill there is provision for conditions to be put on licences. Almost any condition which is germane to a particular situation can be inserted. There is also provision to impose certain monetary penalties for the breach of conditions attached to licences. Previously, in the period between an operator obtaining a licence and having to renew it nothing could be done in this respect. In a situation such as described by the hon. member, where there may be numerous complaints, a condition could be attached to a licence covering the connection fee and if this condition were not observed the operator could lose his licence or be penalized in some other way. But to set tariffs for each individual C.A.T.V. operator, particularly considering the way C.A.T.V. systems have proliferated in the last few years, would not be the proper step.
Hon. members may have seized on this proposed idea as something new but I think they should stop and think about it. Many of the experts in this field, particularly those least friendly to the C.A.T.V. operators, namely the C.A.B. people, would like to scrunch them down, and in turn the C.A.T.V. operators would like to scrunch down private broadcasters.

May I point out that once again the Secretary of State shows she does not understand C.A.T.V. operations. She states that the C.A.B. wants to scrunch the C.A.T.V. people, whatever that means. This is true enough, but C.A.T.V. operators do not want to scrunch the television operators because it is from them that they get the programs they sell to the public. I wish she understood C.A.T.V.

The point raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming is worthy of attention by the committee. I am interested in the
6318	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting explanation of the situation given by the Secretary of State. If I understand it correctly, a definition of what constitutes a broadcasting undertaking is before us in a way that we have not had it defined since the establishment of community antenna television systems.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lapointe deals with the charges for advertising by broadcasters in the radio and television field. I certainly agree that there does not seem to have been any serious interest in many quarters in setting up a tariff structure in this area. On the other hand, many of us have been aware of abuses on the part of the community antenna television systems in various parts of the country. Heretofore this has not been a matter under the control of any regulatory broadcasting authority.
I believe the suggestion of the Secretary of State that there is provision for conditions to be attached to licences, if it is germane to the question of hook-up fees, monthly rates and so on, should be gone into pretty carefully by the regulatory body to see how they can deal with this matter in laying down the conditions of the licence. Many persons claim that what has in certain instances been a real abuse of a monopoly situation should not be allowed to continue under the aegis of the public authority which is being set up by parliament. I would be content for the present at least to wait and see whether the procedure suggested by the Secretary of State could be developed to meet the situation brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Timiskaming.

Mr. Chairman, the Secretary of State tells us that the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Lapointe is not new to her and that this matter has been fully considered by herself and by the officials of her department. There is no reason for us to doubt that. However, even to those members of the house who were members of the broadcasting committee it comes as a bolt out of the blue. It certainly would appear to have great ramifications and implications. Yet it is brought before us as sort of spontaneous ejaculation which we should deal with here and now. I suggest it would not be asking too much to request that this matter be held in abeyance until Monday.
We have had some debate concerning the necessity and/or desirability of this proposal.

DEBATES	February 2, 1968
At first glance this would seem to be a desirable course of action to take inasmuch as there are quite a number of smaller cities and larger towns in Canada with only one television station which has a monopoly. One can argue, of course, that advertisers are not necessarily at a disadvantage because they can resort to other media such as the press, handbills and so on, as the hon. member for York-Humber has suggested. It is true that if there is not intramedia competition one can point to the intermedia competition and say that someone wishing to rent time for the purpose of political broadcasting can always resort to another means of communication. I am wondering how realistic that kind of argument is.
I do not wish to take up much time because I realize the hon. lady is becoming impatient. I certainly do not blame her. However, in this instance I hope she will be lenient and allow this matter to be held over so that it can be considered properly. If we must vote on the amendment this afternoon I suppose I will have to vote against it. Much as I like the principle of the idea, I would have to vote against it simply on the basis that something as important as this should not be dealt with so casually.
There is another argument in respect of the amendment which I believe should be considered. If we attempt to give the council regulatory powers in this regard I see certain difficulties. If we stipulate that the council shall have the power to set maximum fees, this could be construed as an invitation to do so. If we do not do that and say instead that the council shall have the power to adjudicate in respect of rate increases after the coming into force of this bill, which would be another way to deal with the matter, then what is to stop the television interests in these one-channel or one-station towns increasing their rates in the interval? Finally, it has been suggested by one of my colleagues that if we attempt to regulate it might be that the major advertisers would seek and probably make arrangements with the television station owner for a bonus system and so on. There are different ways by which to get around any regulation. I would hope that the hon. lady would see the sense in holding this over at least until Monday.

Mr. Chairman, I feel the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schreyer) made a reasonable and moderate appeal to the Secretary of State, asking her to allow that

clause to stand. Obviously, we shall not dispose of this bill today. Therefore, there is no objection to suspending the study of that clause or to deferring it until later. When the Secretary of State asked yesterday to pass quickly all the non-contentious clauses, in an attempt to speed up the discussion of the bill, we readily agreed, even though it was done very hastily and it did not seem to us to be the best procedure. I wonder why the Secretary of State does not agree to the suggestion just made, all the more so because the discussion on this bill will no doubt continue on Monday.
If the hon. Secretary of State would accept to co-operate, I am convinced that she would receive in return the same co-operation from the members.
Mr. Chairman, a great many points have not been well explained. With the proper explanations, perhaps everyone would be in favour of that amendment. The hon. Secretary of State tells us that the proposition was considered by her officials and turned down. It would be interesting to know why, and the hon. minister has not told us. We do not know why the officials have turned down such an idea. What I find most surprising, is the fact that the minister seems to think that it would require a whole new administrative structure. But the same administrative structure is found in all the areas where there is a monopoly, and sometimes a larger staff is needed. Let us take, for instance, the field of truck transportation where the structure is considerably more complex than that which would be necessary in this case.
That is why I think that the amendment should be accepted, and I ask the hon. Secretary of State to tell us whether or not she is prepared to accept this matter to be put off until Monday?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, this bill has already, I think, taken more time than anything except the flag debate and possibly the debate on the Canada Pension Plan. My hon. friend is quite wrong when he says I suggested that we should pass the non-contentious clauses. That suggestion came from the house leader of the Conservative party, not from me. I acceded to it with the hope that we would get one or two of them passed.
It may be true that we will be talking about this on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of next week, or perhaps for another four
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting or five weeks. The hon. member apparently has nothing else to do than impede the business of the country. He has said clearly that it is his intention to destroy the country and he is now starting, with the assistance of the hon. member for York-Humber, to destroy parliament. This is a pretty good way of doing so, but he is not going to have my co-operation in his efforts. So far as I am concerned, I do not see any reason why a bill which has been studied publicly and privately for almost four years now should be stood further.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not reply to the remarks of the hon. Secretary of State. I am not in the habit of quibbling about anything whatsoever, with so nice a lady. I would rather capitulate when I find myself in that kind of situation. However, with regard to the bill, I should like to add a few remarks.
I noticed that the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schreyer) said that, at first glance, he finds the bill quite acceptable, and that the only reason which could induce him to vote against it, is that he does not know all its implications.
First of all, I should like to point out to him that the field of radio and television is the only one where, while there is a state-imposed monopoly, rates do not come under regulations. To my mind, this is already a sufficient reason to at least accept the principle that the state, having set up by law monopolies in certain areas of the country, should now prevent exploitation of the public by regulating the prices.
The member for Springfield also wonders what would happen in the field of business. I would like to tell him that, in the areas with no competition and where owners of television stations enjoy a practical monopoly, where prices are high, only the great nation-wide companies operating throughout the country and able to provide an adequate budget can use television for advertising. The small producers, the small businessmen, the small industrialists do not have the same means, so they cannot meet excessive prices.
One might say that all they have to do is select another medium of advertising. Possibly, but today, in the business world, the winner is the one who uses all advertising media. If an advertising medium as important
February 2, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting as television is eliminated, if the small businessmen are deprived thereof, this means that they are being discriminated against and monopolies created by the state through legislation are allowed to crush the small operator who cannot use television programs.
Television stations set their rates rather arbitrarily, according to the ratings. When there are two television stations in an area, rates become competitive and are less likely to increase.
When there is only one station, rates are set arbitrarily and small businessmen are the ones hard hit. I could give examples of abusive rates of television stations. Devious methods are used and a board could prevent such abuse.
In the field of political programs, for instance, the television station in Quebec will no longer sell 15-minute periods for $300. They prefer to divide those 15 minutes in three periods of five minutes, each selling for $200. Thus divided the 15-minute period costs $600, whereas if sold as a whole it would bring in only $300. They refuse to sell 15-minute periods even if all the political parties were willing to pay for uninterrupted periods. All parties without exception have to accept those conditions because during an election campaign the owners of those stations say: Let us get the most out of this while it lasts. And since the going is good and they want to take advantage of it, they find a way to increase the prices.
I know that at the Quebec television station, for example, simply to screen a film or a video-tape of 15 minutes, they charge $80. This is a means of overcharging, and even if that is not acceptable, there is no alternative because there is only one television station in Quebec which sells time to political programs and it is a private station.
The C.B.C. does not sell such time. There is no choice; people are forced to submit to a monopoly created by legislation and by a federal government council. This monopoly is allowed to exist while in every other field, monopolies have been prohibited without there being at the same time limitations on prices to prevent the fleecing of the public.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. Secretary of State told us, a while ago, that for the first time the bill contains a provision allowing the Canadian radio-television commission to set up regulations authorizing it, when licences come up for renewal, to impose fines, penalties and even to suspend licences when the regulations have not be complied with.

I hope that it will be possible to include in the regulations of the Canadian radio-television commission a provision on maximum fees, on rates and the conditions to be complied with before increasing the rates for commercials.
If the Secretary of State were tell us that there is a method to include in the regulations of this Canadian radio-television commission such a principle or such a notion, then we would be happy. Half a loaf is better than no loaf. Is the Secretary of State agreeable to the inclusion, in these regulations of the commission, of a provision dealing with increases in fees by the radio and television stations?
Then, we could simply confirm the principle that the commission is empowered to make regulations. Would the minister accept such an amendment enabling the commission to an enact such regulations?
I see that the minister will not listen to anything further on this bill. Well, at least I was able to make my suggestion, but I am opposed to the fact that a state monopoly is allowed without at the same time setting limits to the exploitation of the public.

Mr. Chairman, there is one word of subclause (iii) of clause 16 I should like to draw to the attention of the committee. Clause 16 reads:
In furtherance of Its objects, the council, on the recommendation of the executive committee, may-
It then sets out that the council may make regulations applicable to persons holding broadcasting licences, or to persons holding broadcasting licences of one or more classes respecting, as stated in subclause (iii)-
-the proportion of time that may be devoted to the broadcasting of programs, advertisements or announcements of a partisan political character and the assignment of such time on an equitable basis to political parties and candidates,
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am a member of the broadcasting committee and I well remember the lengthy discussion which took place on the white paper which was put before us by the Department of the Secretary of State some time ago, and on which we were supposed to express our opinions. As hon. members know, the committee endorsed 19 out of 21 paragraphs of
February 2, 1968
the white paper. An argument arose on subclause (d) of clause 2 of the bill which reads:
It is hereby declared that
(d) the programming provided by the Canadian Broadcasting System should be varied and comprehensive and should provide reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy, -
The suggestion was made that the subclause should read:
-should provide equitable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy, -
A lengthy discussion ensued in the committee on the use of the words "equitable" and "reasonable". With reference to clause 16 (b)(iii) I should like to refer to the political argument which developed. Half a dozen members of the broadcasting committee referred to the situation in the United States where there is a regulation affecting T.V. stations and radio, according to which all candidates for the presidency must be given equal time on both these media. I should like to refer to a specific instance during an election when there were two or three of what are generally called nuisance candidates running for the presidency of the United States of America. One of them at least was straightforward enough to state that the reason he was running for the presidency of the United States was that only in this way would he be able to appear on the national network. This strikes people as being absolutely ridiculous, namely that a man who might be able to garner only about a thousand votes in all of the United States should be given equal time to present whatever platform he claims to have advocated, as against such historical organizations as the Republican and Democratic parties. The discussion with regard to the word "reasonable" on subclause 2(d) went on for a long time, but at the end the committee agreed that the word "reasonable" was much more appropriate.
