speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, early in the debate I indicated in private to the Secretary of State that I thought there was one serious lack in the bill in that, under its terms we as members of parliament would no longer have any means of influencing the new broadcasting authority either directly or indirectly, and that we could not convey public opinion to the broadcasting authority. Therefore I felt it was absolutely necessary for us to provide somewhere in the bill for the formation of regional advisory councils. My suggestion was that this provision should be made in clause 2 of the bill where the objectives of the broadcasting system are outlined, but my suggestion was not accepted by the minister and consequently I did not press for an amendment to clause 2.
However, upon reflection I am more convinced than ever that we would be remiss in

6322	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting our duties in the house if we did not establish some sort of regional councils. The white paper on broadcasting made reference at page 9 to the feasibility and desirability of setting up regional broadcasting councils to advise upon representations made by the general public with regard to programming. I suggest that if we are to provide some means to the public whereby the force of public opinion may make itself felt, we must add a provision after subclause 16 (c).
I therefore propose the following amendment:
That clause 16 be amended by adding after subclause (c) an additional subclause (d) as follows:
"(d) establish regional advisory councils in order that it shall have the benefit of the advice of as broad as possible a range of Canadian public opinion."
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I do not believe any of us here would deny, or very few would deny that over the years there have been abuses committed by our national broadcasting system, especially in recent years in the area of public affairs. I do not intend to discuss that subject at length because it has been discussed at length by members during the last few days. It is my firm conviction that the C.B.C. has immunized itself from the democratic process. I ask members, especially those on the government side, to hear me out on my proposal. The amendment does not change the bill in any way. The type of regional council envisaged would be set up in the five geographical regions in Canada, the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario, the prairies, British Columbia and the Northwest Territories. Members would be appointed for two years. They would not receive remuneration. They would be named by a number of organizations which would range from religious groups, educational groups, the labour movement, management, agriculture, political parties and provincial governments to any other major group of public opinion which the broadcasting commission deemed suitably reflected Canadian public opinion.
The advisory council which I envisage obviously would not have the legal power to force the C.B.C. to do anything. It would be our assurance, as members of parliament, that we have not thrown away all protection for the Canadian public in this bill. In fact this is what we would be doing if we passed this bill without an appropriate amendment to establish these regional advisory councils. If we did so we would be, in effect, saying to this broadcasting authority: You have the

DEBATES	February 2, 1968
power in clause 16 with respect to such other matters as you deem necessary for the furtherance of these objectives, to set up these advisory councils. However, I feel that we must do more than that. We must clearly set forth that it is our desire that these regional councils should be set up.
If the minister would go along with it, I would be prepared to settle for one national advisory council. My argument against a national advisory council would be that it would not be possible to reflect adequately the linguistic make-up of the country on that type of council. It would not be possible, for example, to provide representation for native peoples such as would be the case with a regional council.
There are a number of defects in a national advisory council which I think could be overcome with regional councils. I do not want to take up too much time of the committee, but I am convinced it is essential that somewhere in the bill we have an indication that this house insists that such councils be set up. This amendment would make it clear that we expect the commission to establish such regional councils. If this amendment is accepted it would be necessary to make further amendments later in the bill setting out the details as to how the regional advisory councils are to be made up. Perhaps these amendments could be made following clause 21. This would depend on whether or not my amendment is accepted.
The principle of advisory councils has been accepted and put into effect in the United Kingdom, a country whose national broadcasting system is the world's outstanding example of impartiality. In the federal Republic of Germany, with the experience of the world's most appalling dictatorship, they came to the conclusion early that democracy could best be protected if the national broadcasting system were subject to certain checks and safeguards. A system of regional advisory councils based on each of the German states is in effect in Germany and is working well.
The Canadian Association of Broadcasters in what I believe is part of their submission to the standing committee, said they believed that the regulating body should have regional offices and be responsible for the organization of advisory councils composed of individuals and interested organizations. Then they make reference to the fact that the white paper mentioned the possibility of advisory councils. They go on from there to state that the B.B.G. would recommend favourably on this
February 2, 1968

proposal if in the light of experience it felt its own arrangements were inadequate in this respect.
This is not good enough. As members of this house, I suggest it is incumbent upon all of us to make sure there is some means in the Broadcasting Act whereby public opinion can exert itself on the broadcasting authority. If public opinion cannot do so through parliament, how else is it going to do so? Are we going to leave it up to this organization entirely to decide whether or not it shall hear the public? There are provisions for the commission to hear complaints, but this is not good enough. I strongly urge the minister to reconsider her opposition to the concept of regional advisory councils. It is for this reason, Mr. Chairman, I have taken the time of the committee this afternoon. I hope members on this side of the house as well as the other will support the suggestion I have just made.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak briefly on this amendment presented by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Hunting-don-Laprairie. I believe the idea presented in his amendment is a practical and worthwhile one. I have spoken a number of times in this debate about the necessity of providing in this legislation a means by which the management of the publicly owned broadcasting system could assess public opinion. It is very difficult for the members of this house to do so. It is very difficult for the C.B.C. to do so directly. In fact I have been increasingly alarmed over the amount of correspondence that comes to my desk expressing frustration on the part of Canadians who write to the C.B.C. and do not even receive an acknowledgement of their letters, let alone a reasonable reply to the questions raised.
As the hon. member has just mentioned, this type of advisory council is working very well in both the United Kingdom and the Republic of Germany. It was my original intention that a formal council be set up on a national basis, though not appointed by the C.B.C. or by parliament, so as to represent the various democratic organizations in society across the country.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
In considering the proposal in light of this debate, and in view of our responsibility to dispose of the bill as quickly as possible, it seems to me that this type of amendment is probably more fitting at the present time. It would meet the need for a national advisory council just as well. In fact, it could even be
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting more effective because programming policy is geared not only to the national system, but must likewise be geared to regional taste as well. I think therefore that this amendment is a very practical one, as we adapt the idea of an advisory council to the Canadian scene.
I do not intend to speak at length on the amendment but I do commend it both to the committee and the minister. It has a great deal of worth in it. This amendment provides the management of the C.B.C. with a legitimate sounding board of public opinion. The creation of this body would not require great expense; the most expensive item might be holding the occasional meeting. In fact, even this item might not be expensive because I visualize the representatives on these regional councils as representatives of various organizations, and more than likely those organizations would be only too pleased to send their representatives to the council meetings at their own expense.
Some hon. members might ask where these representatives are to come from. Basically I see them coming from most of the democratic organizations in the country, such as home and school associations, university organizations, teachers federations, labour organizations and the Legion. Even representatives of civic clubs and other important and legitimate national organizations, and other private organizations, might attend. I am pleased to give my support to this amendment and I trust that the minister will see fit to accept it without prolonged debate on the worth that I feel it contains.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief observations on the amendment now before the committee. I will vote against if for the following reasons. First of all, I think this national council-we have now changed its name to national commission -has good representation from across Canada, in the same way as the former Board of Broadcast Governors had. That board was composed of members from every part of Canada. If this national commission is set up on the same basis, I see little reason for regional councils to be set up across a country that has a sparse population of 22 million.
Might I ask the hon. member a question. How many members are on the council as constituted?
Fifteen altogether.

Is it the hon. member's opinion that such a body, the members of
February 2, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting which have certain technical and financial qualifications, is able to give the necessary advice on programming that might be required?

My understanding, Mr. Chairman, is that there are 15 members on the national commission. In the second part of my hon. friend's question, he referred to organizations such as home and school associations and similar bodies, and I see no reason why they cannot present their views in letters, briefs or through other means to the national commission. I am one of those who feel we are beginning to have government by boards and commissions. It seems to me that every piece of legislation that comes before the house requires the appointment of a board, commission or council. I think if one is set up in this legislation, that one will be sufficient.
The hon. member who introduced the amendment spoke of the system in operation in Great Britian. Perhaps regional councils are needed in an area that is so densely populated as Britain, but I do not think regional commissions are required in this country, certainly not at this particular stage in the history of our broadcasting and television services. Therefore I would oppose the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, the proposal made by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie relates to the clause that deals with the Canadian radio-television commission, as well as to this clause. The hon. member for Red Deer kept referring to the C.B.C. but the amendment relates to all broadcasting.
I should like to make one or two comments on the amendment. When the director general of the B.B.C. and the director general of the I.T.A. came to Ottawa from the United Kingdom I questioned them on this point, but I have forgotten their answers. This was November 1966 and I am afraid I have not looked at the minutes recently.
However, a perusal of the handbooks of the B.B.C. and the I.T.A. indicates that there are a great many advisory bodies. They have professional advisory bodies for education and religious broadcasting, and there are also a great many regional bodies. These might be useful; I do not know. But I am against setting up bodies which become innocuous, "nothing" bodies that really do not do anything. If I could be persuaded that these advisory commissions in various parts of the country could contribute to better broadcasting in some way, then they might be worth

while, but I do not think the case for that has been proven.
There is one way we could get around this difficulty, Mr. Chairman, and this suggestion was made in the committee. Both the regulatory body and the board of directors of the C.B.C. should be encouraged to meet in different parts of Canada at different times. I know that occasionally this has been done in the past. However, I see the regulatory authority meeting sometimes in Vancouver, sometimes in Regina and sometimes in St. John's to hold a public hearing to find out what the public, either individually or through organizations, thinks about the job that is being done by the broadcasters, public and private.
The board of directors of the C.B.C. should also move around the country. They should advertise the fact that they are holding a meeting at a certain place, and they should invite the public to come and be heard. This might serve the purpose that the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie has in mind. I do know that these bodies have been set up in the United Kingdom, but how active or effective they are I do not know. I have my doubts about them.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I merely wish to continue in the same vein as the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie), and say that the intention of the amendment moved by the member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie (Mr. Watson), strikes me as excellent, but likely to add to the clumsiness of structures which are already cumbersome as it is. The matter was discussed briefly in committee and, for that very same reason, the suggestion that regional committees be set up on a permanent basis was turned down.
I feel, as does the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, that the same object can be achieved through sittings of the Board of Broadcast Governors and the board of directors of the C.B.C., not only if those bodies give notice of their alternate sittings in various parts of the country, but if, to the contrary, notice of these sittings will be given ahead of time and the audience throughout our whole broadcasting system will be invited specifically to present grievances, make representations, and-why not?-offer its congratulations.
This too was mentioned in the committee by the representatives of both the bureau of
February 2, 1968

broadcast governors and the board of the C.B.C., and the two bodies replied to the committee that they had the intention to do so, they thought it essential to act in this way. Such an attitude would serve to avoid what the member for Burnaby-Richmond indicated that there is a risk, if we organize too heavy a superstructure, of having also a dead superstructure. If the bureau of broadcast governors and the board of the C.B.C. announce that they will meet to hear representations from the listeners, then, those who come before them will come of their own free will and not because they have been appointed. They will come because they will have something to say.
If is true that there is so much discontent over broadcasting among Canadians, we should not doubt for a second that the intermediary organizations or voluntary bodies, all kinds of associations including viewers associations will make their representations before these two bodies of their own accord, not because they have to, but because they are motivated by their own feelings and rules of conduct.
So I say that we should drop the proposition now before us in favor of a much more flexible formula and probably therefore a much more efficient one.
{English]

Mr. Chairman, I rise briefly to congratulate the hon. member for introducing this amendment, although I am not quite sure whether it fills the bill entirely. The amendment would seek to provide for the establishment of regional advisory councils in order that the national council shall have the benefit of the advice of as broad as possible a range of public opinion. I think there is merit in this amendment because, at the present time, we have a national council only and it is very difficult to get, shall I say, the response to certain programs or policies of the C.B.C. through the national council alone, or even through this house.
I think this amendment does provide an opportunity to improve the participation of the general public in the administration of this important legislation. As my colleague from Burnaby-Richmond says, this sort of thing has been the practice in Great Britain for a number of years. They have less geographic space to deal with but a larger population. I am in favour of doing everything possible to get the participation of the public in the administration of the laws we pass in this house.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
So far as my own constituency is concerned, I have received in the neighbourhood of 300 letters in connection with C.B.C. programs, and that sort of thing. You see, I represent a riding that is very alert to what is happening in Ottawa, and in other places. I am sure those people in the Kootenays would welcome the opportunity from time to time to bring opinions to the attention of the national council. I know this. I am sure there are many, shall I say, people who would like the opportunity to serve in this capacity on a voluntary basis. If I put it to the people I represent and said, "Are you willing to appoint a regional board to represent and reflect opinion in the Kootenays?" which is quite substantial, many of them would willingly serve on such a board on a voluntary basis, without any expense to the state. It is a matter of getting opinions, recording them, gathering them in and sending them to the national council so that they know what the reaction is in various parts of Canada. I think the hon. member has a point here and I hope some consideration will be given to the idea he has in mind.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie obviously feels the concern which I expressed when I spoke on the bill on December 20. I was intrigued by his phrase, if I heard it correctly, that the C.B.C. in the name of democracy has immunized itself from public opinion. I am inclined to the view that we in this house, by the legislative process, have had a good deal to do with that immunization. In other words, in our zeal to ensure that the broadcasting system does not come under some form of partisan political domination, we have more or less set the C.B.C. to one side in a way that has brought some feeling of frustration to many people in Canada, because of their inability to make felt their feelings and views with respect to the C.B.C.
I do not want to repeat what I said before, but I suggested that the best regional and national forum in Canada is this House of Commons. Outside the actual terms of this bill we, as a house of parliament, have it within our power to set up a mechanism different from that which existed heretofore, and through that mechanism we could make the views of regions known and felt from time to time. We could do that with respect to broadcasting and other related matters, instead of, as we have done in the past, using the Secretary of State as a go-between with ourselves on one side and the broadcasting system on the other.
6326	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
I made references to the technique employed when we established the redistribution commissions. We evolved the machinery for making our views known to them. I draw this proposal to the attention of the hon. member, and my own view is-because it is my own brainchild, I suppose-that that proposal or technique might serve better to meet the purposes he has in mind.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make two comments, one of them about the remarks of the hon. member for Wellington South. He said that the commission would be adequate to reflect public opinion to the broadcasting authority. I do not think it is adequate, and that is why I brought forward this amendment.
I do not think the commission, with its number of members, will be suitably reflective of Canadian public opinion. The hon. member is right. Under the bill the commission will have the resources, if it decides to, to go across the country. It may consult with various bodies across the country. But we have not said, in this bill, that it should do that. If the minister would consent anywhere else in the bill to some amendment which would indicate parliament's desire for this authority to go out among the public and ask how the public feels about broadcasting, I shall be content. If we do not provide for that in the bill somewhere, we shall be remiss in our duty.
The second aspect of the proposed amendment which was touched on by the hon. member for Hochelaga had to do with the clumsiness of the machinery which would be employed under this amendment. I do not think the machinery would be as cumbersome as he imagines.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I envisage that the members of the advisory councils would be volunteers appointed by labour unions, educational groups and so on. They might be paid officials of those unions or other groups, or they might not. In any event, their services would not add, as the hon. member for Hochelaga suggested, to the cost of operation of the national broadcasting authority. Their presence might mean more work for the commission. In fact it would, because the commission would be obliged to consult with them once or twice a year and it would be obliged also to answer for ignoring recommendations by the councils in previous years.

DEBATES	February 2, 1968
I believe it is essential to the working of the democratic process in Canada that we end the isolation of our national broadcasting system from the Canadian public. In my view it is important that we should accept this amendment or, alternatively, that the minister should place some other provision in the bill which would satisfy the objections I have raised-objections which I believe to be legitimate.

I rise to ask whether the hon. member would entertain a question. He began by proposing the establishment of regional advisory groups or councils. From his last few remarks I understood they are to be composed, at least in part of representatives from occupational groups. Is he proposing some new hydrid?

I indicated that if this amendment were passed it would be necessary to bring in an additional amendment later, probably to clause 21, setting out details of the regional councils to be established. I would propose that the members should be appointed for a period not exceeding two years, that the appointments should be non-remunerative, that the councils should be based on regional areas and that their members should include representation from labour unions, educational groups, agriculture, religious groups and so on, the commission having discretion to allow persons to be appointed from any other groups which they felt were adequately representative of Canadian opinion.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprai-rie (Mr. Watson), and I still do.
An advisory council such as that one is obviously justified. The programs of the C.B.C. and of private television stations enter our homes every day, sometimes up to 15 or 16 hours a day. They bring ideas, opinions, information, entertainment and all sorts of things into every home.
It is noted, at the same time, that C.B.C. programs, as one might expect, cause reactions, as evidenced by the number of letters to newspapers about such or such a program. subtopic: FEES FOR PROFESSIONAL SERVICES OF BARRISTER AND SOLICITOR MEMBERS IN PARLIAMENTARY MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has seconded this motion, because I know that at the same time it is seconded by the majority of the members of this house. This is a bill to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act, with the subtitle "St. Luke 11;46". I should like to explain this reference to St. Luke 11;46 which reads as follows:
And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.
It is not usual for a subtitle to be taken from the scriptures, but this statement of our Lord is the first recorded opinion with respect to the gentlemen of the legal profession in the Christian era. I mention this only because of its historical significance to indicate that this problem has been with us for nearly 2,000 years. However, members of the legal profession, like untold millions, have responded to the teachings of the gospel since that time.
Senate and House of Commons Act
My attention was first directed to this question when I first discovered that a few members of parliament, who are also lawyers, were accepting fees from constituents and clients for representations made on their behalf to the ministry on immigration matters or for other services rendered in representations made to other ministries or agencies of the federal government.
In fairness to members of the legal profession, I must say that over a long period of years I have had a very happy relationship with the majority of lawyers I have known in British Columbia, and with a number of the justices of the supreme or county courts of British Columbia, who have all been men of honour and integrity, regardless of the party which appointed them to their high offices.
A code of ethics for the legal profession has concerned the law societies of Canada, various other organizations and the press. For instance, in the Globe and Mail of February 7, 1966, it is reported that the Law Society of Upper Canada has paid over a million and a half dollars as compensation to clients of disbarred lawyers in the past 12 years, according to treasurer John D. Arnup. Included in this report is a list of lawyers who have been disbarred for unethical practices.
I have also been informed of persons who have paid members of parliament, who are also lawyers, for representations made to the ministry of immigration on their behalf. However, these persons naturally do not wish to be identified. In this regard I should like to relate briefly the experience of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott). Three days after I introduced this bill last year one of his constituents phoned him requesting information as to whether a certain relative of his in Europe could be sponsored. The hon. member for Danforth said that he would get in touch with the immigration office. He did so and was told that the case would be examined on the basis of the information given. Later the hon. member received a phone call from the immigration office advising him that the person in question was entitled to come to Canada. They suggested that he advise his constituent to apply at a certain immigration office. When he so advised his constituent the constituent said to him, "I am quite willing to pay you the $500 which is usually charged by members of par Lament for this service." The hon. member for Danforth, being the upright member he is, turned this down, with a snort.

speechtext:
Also because of his high principles.
This problem has also been of some concern to the Congress of the United States and various state legislatures. I am sure many members of parliament have read of the scandal surrounding senator Tom Dodd, a lawyer who used his influence for corrupt purposes. This senator's activities caused the Senate of the United States to pass a censure resolution which is of such interest that I should like to quote it:
Resolved, that it is the judgment of the Senate that the senator from Connecticut, Thomas J. Dodd.. .deserves the censure of the Senate: and he is so censured for his conduct, which is contrary to accepted morals, derogates from the public trust expected of a senator, and tends to bring the Senate into dishonour and disrepute.
I think the Senate acted wisely on that occasion. This problem is of increasing concern to Congress and to state legislatures, as evidenced by the introduction of bills that would deal with conflict of interest and provide for a state ethics commission.
This bill proposes to remedy the grievance that arises when the public relationship between a member of parliament and a citizen is subverted to the private relationship between lawyer and client, to the financial hurt of the citizen. For example, the citizen asks his member to make inquiries of the ministry in an immigration matter and is often dismayed to find that, his member being a lawyer, he is billed for fees on a solicitor-client basis. This grievance is an ancient one, and the remedy proposed is to revive and modernize an order of the United Kingdom that is 300 years old.
Parliament has delegated to the executive the power to grant or refuse in its discretion many matters that once were entrusted to the House of Lords to investigate, hear, and grant or refuse. They were classed as "personal" petitions. The commons delegated the airing and adjudication of these private grievances to the upper chamber by making no rules whereby the petitions could be initiated in the commons.
The commons, on account of the conflict of interest activities of its lawyer-members in intermeddling as lawyers in these private petitions, successively passed orders which placed the activities of these lawyer-members within the control of the commons. I do not have time to deal with the various orders that were passed in the commons of Great Britain to meet this question.

DEBATES	February 2. 1968
[DOT] (5:10	p.m.)
In considering such a bill it is interesting to look into foreign legislation to discover the kind of provisions which have been adopted in other countries. I have read as widely as I could under the circumstances, but this did not permit of much serious reading. I may confess that it is difficult to find legislation of this kind which is more or less analogous with the purposes of this bill, and for two reasons. On the one hand it has been impossible for me to review all foreign acts and regulations, due to the fact that they are not available. On the other hand, according to the documents I have examined, it seems that the subject matters are yet to be considered.
Undoubtedly the concern to ensure the independence of members of parliament in the face of financial, economic and social pressure has become more marked over the years. This is a matter of status seeking, as you will understand. Nevertheless one can find in other countries some provisions regarding the incompatibility of occupation, by which a member of parliament is debarred from following certain occupations during his term of office.
The purpose of this bill is more limited. It does not provide for disqualification from membership of parliament by virtue of occupation. It only contains a suggestion to limit a lawyer's privilege to accept any fee or benefit for acting in certain government affairs. Problems of conflicts of interest, undue influence, and other violations of duty by legislators or other members of the government are being raised in Canada as well as in other countries. We have heard of several cases raised recently in the United States.
In continental Europe the problem of conflicts of interests of the lawyer do not appear clearly solved. This can be understood in Scandinavian countries where parliament does not include a great number of lawyers. As is written by Professor Elis Hastad in "The Parliament of Sweden":
The practice of drawing the representatives of the people from the ranks of their social equals, because they are "the representatives of the brethren at home", is not peculiar to the parliament of Sweden. Much the same occurs in all the other Scandinavian countries. The Swedish Riksdag is no "parliament of lawyers" of the type found in several other European lands, and above all, in the Congress of the United States where at times almost two thirds of the members have been jurists.
February 2, 1968

Also in the Australian parliament, lawyers are not in great number. As written by J. D. B. Miller in "Australian Government and Politics":
The candidates elected from the various parties are less easy to distinguish from one another than might be expected: in speech, dress and standard of education, they mirror the general conditions of Australians. Only a minority has had a tertiary education...
That means an education of sort of third degree level.
The situation is different in some European parliaments which are made up in good part of lawyers. Nevertheless in continental Europe the question of the lawyer-legislator conflict of interest does not seem systematically under control.
There is no doubt that the problems of the professional role of lawyer-members of the Senate and House of Commons in certain government affairs is one of ethics. When the lawyer has a seat in the Commons or in the Senate he does not cease to be a lawyer. In that field his conduct should be governed by the positive rules of legal ethics.
Of course every bar association is governed by its own rules, and it is quite impossible to frame a satisfactory definition of ethics as applied to the legal profession. The sense of honour and fairness should be the same from coast to coast. Although it is hard to limit the exact duties of the lawyer, the Canadian Bar Association approved a statement of some of the ethical principles which should be observed by members of the legal profession.
In February of 1956 the council of the city of Toronto resolved:
That the government of Ontario be requested to enact the necessary legislation to make it clear that a lawyer who is a member of metropolitan council or of any municipal council, shall not be entitled to accept a fee for acting for any person in a matter in which the council of which he is a member may act by resolution or by law-
This resolution was considered as one of legal ethics. The discipline committee brought this matter to the attention of the profession, reminding them that no lawyer can serve two conflicting interests, and if a member of the profession holds any elected or appointed office he should not accept any retainer through which his duty to his client and his duty to such office may conflict.
The British House of Commons has not confined itself to the repression of direct pecuniary corruption. To guard against indirect influence it has forbidden the acceptance of fees by its members for professional
6331
Senate and House of Commons Act services connected with proceedings in parliament. Thus a member is not permitted to practise as counsel before the house or any committee thereof, and it is not consistent with parliamentary usage for members to advise, as counsel, upon any private bill or other proceeding in parliament, or matters related to the jurisdiction of parliament.
It has also been declared contrary to the law and usage of parliament for any member to be engaged, either by himself or any partner, in the management of private bills before either house of parliament for pecuniary reward and, upon the same grounds, it was ordered on November 6, 1666:
That such members of this house as are of the Long-Robe shall not be counsel on either side, in any bill depending in the Lords' House, before such bill shall come down from the Lords' House to this house.
The acceptance, in my opinion, by a member of either house of a fee, compensation, gift or reward for drafting, advising upon or revising any bill, petition or other document submitted or intended to be submitted to either house or any committee thereof would appear to be a breach of privilege.
I have referred to the things I have gathered together in respect of this bill because I am serious in this regard, and I have strong support. Several members of the cabinet endorse the principle outlined in this bill, including the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), who has stated strongly that he considers it immoral for any member of parliament to receive any payment for acting as a lawyer in any matter he should undertake as his responsibility as a member of parliament. I also have the strong support of the Secretary of State (Miss La-Marsh) in this regard, and I know of several other members of the cabinet who agree with the principles of this bill. Surely it is necessary at this time to indicate to the Canadian people that we are men of integrity in this house and intend to stand in favour of a code of ethics, so far as our practice is concerned.
In addition I have a letter from Eight Hon. John Diefenbaker which I wish to place on record. I give him credit for the fact that when he was first elected he told me he informed his firm that while he was a member of parliament no member of his firm was to deal with a matter that was within the jurisdiction of parliament or its elected representatives, because he was elected by the people to serve that purpose. That has been his practice and the practice of his firm since.
6332	COMMONS
Senate and House of Commons Act This is what Mr. Diefenbaker said in his letter of April 16, 1966:
Dear Bert:
Your report from parliament hill for April 20th is a very interesting one. I commend you for the stand taken that any law firms with members of parliament therein, ought not to receive fees fpr work which ordinarily should be done by the member in the discharge of his duties.
I know there are members of all parties in parliament who support the principle of this bill. I have received a good number of letters from members of the legal profession in the country informing me of their support. I have also had conversations with many of these people and know they are behind this principle. It is my belief from the letters I have received from members of my constituency, numbering possibly close to 100, that there has been excellent response from the public. Among these letters I received one from His worship Mayor William Dennison of Toronto.
I look forward to hearing the opinions of other members on this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this bill. At the outset let me say I entirely support the principle expressed by the hon. member. I agree that a lawyer should not become involved in any matter which may bring about a conflict of interest betwen his duties as a member of parliament and his position as a lawyer. But having said that, I must go on to the next matter, and that is that with the increasing involvement of the federal government in the everyday business of people, an involvement which did not exist in previous years, it is becoming more and more difficult for a lawyer who works in a firm, or who practises at all, to disengage himself completely from some involvement with the federal government.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I myself practise law on week ends, on holidays, when the house recesses, on an occasional day off, or when my hard working partner wishes to go on a holiday, and I find this involvement is becoming more and more difficult for me. Of course, as parliament sits for longer and longer periods, the opportunity for me to practise law is decreasing. Nevertheless the same difficulty applies as regards my firm, and I feel that it is just as much bound by this bill as I am, myself. We have come to a definite agreement in our firm that we will handle nothing having to do with the federal government in any way.
[Mr. Herridge.l
DEBATES	February 2, 1968
However, what do we do when we handle the estate of a deceased person? This is the backbone of the practice of rural lawyers and a good many urban ones also. There are three things to be done when a person dies: We have to probate his will, which involves a circuit court; we have to file provincial succession duty returns in most provinces, which involves filing a provincial return; and we have to file an estate tax return. This is where the problem lies. Are we barred completely as a law firm from acting on the estate of any deceased person? To what extent are we permitted, according to legal ethics, to file estate tax returns, and to what point are we entitled to press a disputed claim?
We have applied a rule of thumb to it and-and I say this badly-I think most other firms do as well. We feel we are not in any way disqualified from acting on any estate which involves a routine filing of an estate tax return to the federal government, or a routine assessment or even reassessment of property, because no conflict arises in such cases. Nevertheless this lurking problem is at the back of our minds all the time.
There is another problem also. In many small law practices assistance is given in preparing income tax returns. In most cases it is a routine matter, but sometimes a dispute arises and one's client may come back and say "You helped me fill the forms out, and you filled them out wrong". If returns are filled out in our office and a dispute arises, we may have to appear before a federal board of some kind. In such a situation we hand the matter over to someone else.
These are two examples of the difficulties which are brought about by the gradual intrusion of the federal government into the life of the average citizen, and in spite of my absolute agreement with the principle of the bill, I say it is not easy to define the dual role which may be played by a member of parliament; and I am not sure the bill deals adequately with it.
I note that at the end of the bill the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) assigns to Mr. Speaker a discretionary power to set down rules within which the legal profession may act. Perhaps this may be a way out. Speaking for myself, I go home on many week ends and I find my appointment book filled with the names of people who have made inquiries during the week. I have no idea whether they wish to see me on legal
February 2, 1968

or on political business. When they start telling me their story and they reach a point at which there seems to be something involving the federal government, 1 ask them whether they wish to consult me as a lawyer or as a member of parliament. They ask me what the difference is, and I tell them that if they are consulting me as a member of parliament I cannot charge them anything. They say then "That's for me; I will consult you in that capacity". This may often lead such people into traps, because if they have become involved in some family matter in which they may require assistance, which I cannot give because of my position as member of parliament, I merely send them to someone else.
I point these matters out to indicate the difficulties faced by members of parliament who are practicing lawyers. I think that the purpose of the bill is good, and I would have no hesitation in supporting it, but I am sure that all hon. members who are practising lawyers would very much like to have some of these problems cleared up.
In conclusion I should like to say one thing.
I think there should be no difficulty in the open and shut cases, when a lawyer is consulted and attempts to advise a client on a matter dealing directly with the federal government, such as immigration matters in which there is a direct appeal to a government body. In such cases the government body dealing with it is placed in a difficult position because the member of parliament-lawyer may harass the department as a solicitor, and also worry it as a member of parliament. In this event the poor official gets knocked on both sides. In such cases I believe the proposal in the bill can easily be applied. I think that the other matters can work themselves out, and certainly if the bill comes to a vote I will support it.

I know that most bar associations, especially the bar association of the province of Quebec, are quite conscious of the fact some lawyers have done things which are not in accordance with good ethics. Now, one might ask why, since parliament is sitting so often now and since members received a pay increase several years ago, members would want to charge their constituents for the work they are doing with government boards, and so on. I have referred to the fact that a few years ago the salaries of members of parliament were increased. Although I was not here at that time and had no intention of coming here, I supported the policy of increasing the salaries of members of parliament. I thought such a move would prevent these abuses. I thought if members were paid a decent salary, and expenses, they would not be tempted to work outside the house on other matters. I thought, too, that if you paid members low salaries you favoured the wealthier class in society who would be able to run for parliament, whereas those on lower incomes with large families could not afford to maintain a residence in Ottawa and a residence in their constituency. Every time it was thought appropriate to increase the salary of this level of civil servant or judge, you would automatically increase the salaries of members of parliament. This would take members' salaries out of the controversial area in which they have been. I am not suggesting that this be done now. The things you have to do for a constituent often involve legal or quasi legal procedures. Perhaps a lawyer has some advantage over any other type of person in doing these things because he has been dealing with boards and courts before he came to parliament. However, I believe a member should make it clear to his constituent that he does not receive payment for his work.
However, sometimes constituents come to you and want something done quickly. They want you to spend money. If you have to spend money to get something done, perhaps draft procedures for them or make long distance phone calls, then I believe you should make it clear to them that if there are expenses involved which cannot be covered by your parliamentary expenses the client would have to pay the expenses. Members should discourage clients from giving any fee.
All this involves the member of parliament functioning as some sort of ombudsman for his constituents. He should be able to do this in a much more efficient way than he does now. Really, the member of parliament has two functions. His first function is as a legislator, that is the preparation of government programs for the people. His other function is to act as a representative of the people in his constituency vis-a-vis the government and government agencies.

I submit that right now there are some inconsistencies in connection with the help given to members in doing this work. The member who represents the constituency of York-Scarborough, which is the largest constituency in Canada from the point of view of population, has only one secretary, as has the hon. member who, without casting any reflections upon him, represents !les-de-la Madeleine which has about 14,000 constituents. Both members have the same office help and one secretary apiece, as have other members with the exception of ministers. It is a well known fact that members with large constituencies sometimes handle three or four times the correspondence of other members, in their second function as a member of parliament, and to do this work well they should have more help.
In the province of Quebec the provincial members are now given an additional expense account to maintain a secretary in their constituency. This is also the practice in the United States. Some members of the house have suggested from time to time that members of parliament should have offices in their constituency situate in a federal building, such as a post office or other building. A secretary based at this office could assist the constituents of the member and help do a better job to represent them in parliament. Right now this job is not always done as well as it should be.
Only last year, Mr. Speaker, members were given the right to charge for telephone calls made to their constituency. Previously members who lived in the far reaches of Canada had been receiving bills for $60 or $70 a month for telephone calls to their constituency. This has now been changed and members may phone their constituency at government expense.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not my bill, but the bill of the hon. member for Kootenay West. However, I certainly support that suggestion and it was my intention to raise that point. Not only lawyers could charge for their time in dealing with other matters; the same applies to accountants and other professions. Accountants have a lot of experience with income tax and revenue matters and in this respect are in the same position as lawyers. I do not know whether the hon. member for Kootenay West has found that other professions have abused their role as members of parliament by charging their constituents for services rendered, but I think everyone should be included in this measure of reform.
There are members of other professions who take advantage of their position as members of the House of Commons to make money in one way or another. The clause should also be amended to put these persons in the same position as notaries, barristers and solicitors. I do not think it is fair just to limit it to lawyers, though perhaps they have been the chief violators or abusers of their role. I think this is unfortunate because lawyers have been the leaders of reform in this area as well. They have been very conscious that their position as lawyers often leaves them open to situations where they could enter into dishonest or questionable activity. Because many lawyers are aware of this they have gone a long way to discipline the members of their profession and to take care of situations like this.
In conclusion, I support this bill, though I do not think it is a complete remedy of the evil that the hon. member attempts to eliminate.

Personally I have never made a charge for any assistance that I have rendered in immigration cases, and I hope that this will continue to be the case. I agree with the apparent attitude toward the bill taken by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker). In my opinion the bill is certainly discriminatory and I think this should be the opinion of all hon members. Why, for example, should it

Let me take the case of an engineer who is a sitting member. Let us say he is asked to deal with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Is not his position on all fours with the position of the barrister or solicitor?
However, I do agree that the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is useful in that it brings this matter forward for discussion. I agree with the statement in the explanatory notes that a grievance does arise if a member of parliament makes a charge in an immigration case when he is doing nothing more than giving assistance as a politician. Many immigration cases require a great deal of legal assistance.
I encounter this all the time in connection with the admission of people from the Orient. Many problems arise that often require long and detailed research. Birth certificates, marriage certificates and death certificates are required.
In China there is a custom that if a mother loses her child she replaces it with the child of another woman, even concealing the fact from her husband. There are all kinds of permutations and combinations that arise in immigration matters. Blood tests are taken by the department that often indicate that the child in question could not be the child of the parents. Radiological tests sometimes show that the bones of a child indicate that the child is too old to be the one referred to in the application. A member has to advise and assist a constituent who seeks to bring in such a person. Such constituent may have been making monthly payments for the support of the child for years, and he then discovers that the blood test shows that the child is not his.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
A member of parliament does not have time, particularly if he is a full time member, to be of assistance in hard immigration cases; so it is only right and proper to call in the assistance of a solicitor, preferably from the constituent's own community. You have to call in a lawyer in many cases, if you are wise, to communicate with the constituents clearly.


I am out of sympathy with this bill and I agree with the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Aiken) when he says that this bill is far too all embracing. It covers the waterfront. A lawyer, if this bill becomes law, will no longer be able to wind up his legal practice properly. I have been elected for six years and I am still executor for some estates. There are still accounts to pass, payments to look after and investments to take care of. I still have some commitments to companies and only gradually am I able to divest myself of them. This bill would bar a solicitor in my position from accepting any fee, directly or indirectly, or any benefit, as the result of acting in his professional capacity in respect of any matter, wheresoever originating, that is or is intended to be a private or public proceeding in the Senate or House of Commons or in committee of either house or that is, under an act of parliament, within the discretion of a minister of the crown or the governor in council to determine.
How far does that go? In many cases this bill would create grave anxiety and worry to a practising solicitor. I have continued to be a member of the Law Society of Upper Canada; I still have to pay $130 a year, so long as I am doing anything by way of legal practice. It is necessary to keep up a library and to pay the various law association dues. Generally, in the case of a partnership, it is necessary to play ball with your partners.
I have never heard it suggested that we should stop farmers from farming, car dealers from selling cars, consulting engineers from charging, doctors, who are hon. members, from practising medicine-

I suspect that the mover of the bill, who is often referred to as the Baron of the Kootenays, garners in the harvest from his vast holdings in the Columbia river basin, despite his being a highly honourable and respected member of parliament. I was shocked to learn that in the past there were a few cases where members of parliament, who were only part time members at that time, were charging exorbitant and unconscionable fees for the exercise of their political influence. That did not happen often and I do not think it is happening today at all.
